title: [Update] My Claude-built spearfishing game is waiting on Steam review, so I put a free beta on itch.io. Here's what the numbers taught me so far
author: Panda5Studio
selftext:
This is the third post in my series about building a game with AI tools. Claude writes the code (Godot), Codex makes the concept art, and Tripo3D turns that art into 3D models.  
Technically Fishing is a first-person spearfishing game. You dive, spear fish, haul them up, and sell them at the guild. While the Steam build waits for review, I put a free beta (Mac / Windows, about 90 minutes of play) on itch.io.  
Honest numbers so far (screenshot attached):  
76 page views in 30 days  
8 downloads  
Most of my outside visitors came from Reddit. Inside itch, hardly anyone finds the game.  
Someone on r/itchio gave me blunt and very useful feedback: people decide from the first lines of the description, then the screenshots, then the trailer. My screenshots were all scenery, and the progression was buried in a wall of text. So I rewrote the top of the page. The click-through rate inside itch went from under 2% to about 5.6% over the next few days. The sample is tiny, so I'm not calling it proof yet. Next I'm reshooting the screenshots to show what you actually do on a dive.  
They also said it reads like "first-person 3D Dave the Diver." Fair. No sushi bar, though.  
Questions for anyone who has shipped on itch:  
What actually moved your downloads: the page, the trailer, devlogs, or posting elsewhere?  
Is a web build essentially required for people to try a beta on itch?  
For an AI-assisted project, do you mention the tools on the store page, or only in dev posts like this?  
Beta: [https://dept47-games.itch.io/technically-fishing](https://dept47-games.itch.io/technically-fishing)
